newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Crossair mulls new European airline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Crossair mulls new European airline.

text.p: Swiss airline Crossair AG, busy digesting last year's explosive growth, is considering creating a new carrier to get aound EU restrictions and compete on French domestic routes.

Regional airline Crossair, part of SAirGroup, in January founded European Continental Airways (ECA) in the French town of St. Louis, near Basle, with a group of French investors from the travel industry in Mulhouse.

Moritz Suter, Crossair's energetic chief executive, told a news conference that ECA could operate from Basle-Mulhouse airport, which has the unique status of being both in EU-member France and non-EU member Switzerland.
However, Suter stressed ECA was only the working title for the project and it would become clearer by the middle of the year whether it would take shape after talks between the EU and Switzerland.
Crossair has taken a 35 percent in ECA's initial share capital of 250,000 French francs ($43,100).

Italy recently revoked Crossair's rights to fly between Basle and Rome, but by participating in a French-owned company, Crossair could take advantage of Europe's liberalised skies and service Italian cities, Suter said.
"We could not do the same from Zurich or Geneva because they are within Swiss jurisdiction," Suter said.
Another reason for founding ECA in France was that landing and passenger fees for domestic airlines, such as Air France, in Paris was much less than for Swiss airlines.

Crossair's net profit in 1996 jumped 32 percent to 23 million Swiss francs ($15.6 million) and revenue soared 59 percent to 738 million as it took over Swissair's aircraft with capicity for fewer than 100 passengers and short-haul charter operations.

Crossair, which benefits from lower costs than Swissair -- the core airline in SAirGroup -- has mushroomed in recent years. In 1996 its aircraft fleet rose to 62 from 49 and the number of passengers carried jumped to 3.2 million from 2.1 million.

The liberalisation in Europe has lead to a 39 percent fall in revenue per passenger from 1991 to 1996 to 43 cents, but Crossair has remained ahead of the game be cutting its costs per seat offered by 47 percent to 20 cents, Suter said.
"Despite the strong decline in revenue, our break-even point has been falling," Suter said.
Crossair, however, could not quite fill all the 66 percent rise in seats offered in 1996 so the load factor, or utilisation of flights, eased to 49 percent from 53 percent.
"The load factor in Crossair's scheduled flights is not satisfactory, but in light of the increase in seating capacity, it's actually not that bad," Suter said.
Crossair will continue to work on reducing its costs and also scrap some unprofitable routes in 1997.
Despite the anticipated consolidation of growth in 1997, Crossair is budgeting for another 13 percent rise in flights to 138,000 and passengers transported would rise to 4.5 million.
Business in the first quarter of 1997 was already ahead of expectations due to the beneficial impact of the weaker Swiss franc against other European currencies, Suter said.
Sales in 1997 are expected to rise to around 800 million francs and this should boost operating profits.

"However, with lower revenues likely to derive from ancillary sources, our net result is likely to remain largely at 1996 levels," Crossair said, adding that sales of used aircraft are likely be down from 1996 as the fleet is now among the youngest in Europe.
